work: Theophilus, De diversis artibus, Liber I, complete contiguous chapters I–IX
historical_date: Twelfth-century work with early medieval manuscript witnesses; exact wording below follows Hendrie 1847. No direct diplomatic collation of I.1–9 against a medieval folio was obtained in this bounded task.

edition.text_normalization: Join print line breaks and hyphenation; preserve lexical forms. HTML collation corrected only the documented facias/facies and lecenti/recenti discrepancies to the natively viewed print.

scope_boundary: Starts at Caput I after the prologue; ends at the final per omnia of Caput IX, before Caput X. All nine intervening chapters are included. This is a bounded connected source section, not the entire manual or a claim of one historical paragraph.
image_status: The text gives detailed instructions for painting body-image regions. No completed painting is claimed to be the owned output of these chapters. Three medieval witness-page images were viewed, but show the prologue and later chapters rather than I.1–9.
role_distinctions: a material batch or selected portion
a deposited layer on an image

chapters.title: De temperamento colorum in nudis corporibus.
chapters.latin_complete_normalized: COLOR qui dicitur membrina, quo pinguntur facies et nuda corpora, sic componitur. Tolle cerosam, id est album, quod fit ex plumbo, et mitte eam non tritam, sed ita ut est siccam, in vas cupreum vel ferreum, et pone super prunas ardentes, et combure donec convertatur in flavum colorem. Deinde tere eum, et admisce ei albam cerosam et cenobrium, donec carni similis fiat. Quorum colorum mixtura in tuo sit arbitrio; ut si, verbi gratia, rubeas facies habere vis, plus adde cenobrii; si vero candidas, plus appone albi; si autem pallidas, pro cenobrio modicum prasini.
materials_written: cerosa: explicitly white material made from lead
quantity_or_endpoint_qualifiers_written: cerosa initially dry and not ground
mixture of colors at the maker's discretion
pale faces: a little prasinum in place of cenobrium
tools_carriers_or_substrates_written: painted faces and nude bodies; no general binder or vehicle is stated
ordered_claim_inventory: Introduce the name membrina for the color used on painted faces and nude bodies.
Take dry unground cerosa, explicitly described as white made from lead; put in a copper or iron vessel on burning coals.
Heat until it becomes yellow; then grind it.
Add white cerosa and cenobrium until flesh-like.
Leave mixture proportions to the maker and state three complexion alternatives: more cenobrium for red, more white for white, little prasinum instead of cenobrium for pale.

references.referent: the preparation defined in this chapter
cerosa before heating
heated material
references.type: material anaphor with changing grammatical wording

uncertainties: No fixed numerical ratio is supplied.
The edition footnote at cenobrium reads: Vel sinopidem, ex C. R. This is an editorial witness alternative, not a simultaneously required ingredient.
The precise historical identity of cenobrium or prasinum is not inferred from modern chemistry.

chapters.title: De colore prasino.
chapters.latin_complete_normalized: QUI prasinus, est confectio quaedam habens similitudinem viridi coloris et nigri, cujus natura talis est, quod non teritur super lapidem, sed missus in aquam resolvitur et per pannum diligenter colatur, cujus usus in recenti muro pro viridi colore satis utilis est.
materials_written: prasinus, described as a preparation resembling green and black
quantity_or_endpoint_qualifiers_written: quite useful as green on a fresh wall
tools_carriers_or_substrates_written: stone, explicitly excluded as grinding surface for this material
ordered_claim_inventory: Describe prasinus as a preparation resembling green and black.
State that it is not ground on stone; put it into water, dissolve it and carefully strain through cloth.
State its usefulness as green on a fresh wall.

references.referent: prasinum named at the end of I.1

uncertainties: The source does not give prasinus's complete chemical constituents; this input remains a named historical preparation.
The web transcription reads lecenti; native print reads recenti.

chapters.title: De posc primo.
chapters.latin_complete_normalized: CUM vero membrinam miscueris inde facies et nuda corpora impleveris, admisce ei prasinum et rubeum, qui comburitur ex ogra, et modicum cenobrii, et confice posc, ex quo designabis supercilia et oculos, nares, et os, mentum, et fossulas circa nares, et tempora, rugas in fronte et collo, et rotunditatem faciei, barbas juvenum et articulos manuum et pedum, et omnia membra, quae distinguuntur in nudo corpore.
quantity_or_endpoint_qualifiers_written: membrina already mixed and used to fill faces and nude bodies
tools_carriers_or_substrates_written: previously painted faces and nude bodies; no new vessel, binder or general support stated
ordered_claim_inventory: Presuppose that membrina has been mixed and used to fill faces and nude bodies.
Add prasinum, red burned from ochre and a little cenobrium to it.
Name the resulting preparation posc.
Use that preparation to delineate every application locus enumerated below.

chapters.title: De veneda in oculis ponenda.
chapters.latin_complete_normalized: DEINDE commisce nigrum cum modico albo, qui color vocatur veneda, et imple pupillas oculorum. Adde ei etiam de albo amplius, et imple oculos ex utraque parte, et album simplex linies inter pupillam et ipsum colorem, et cum aqua lavabis.
tools_carriers_or_substrates_written: water used in the final wash
ordered_claim_inventory: Mix black with a little white; call the color veneda.
Fill the depicted pupils with it.
Add more white to that color and fill the eyes on both sides.
Draw plain white between the pupil and that color.
Wash with water.

the locally introduced color

uncertainties: The source's pupilla/oculus terminology is preserved rather than converted into a modern anatomical drawing specification.
Prepared paint and applied color are related material uses, not the same individual physical portion.
The final wash has no stated volume, duration or further chemical effect.
